Atlas/Physics

The rules underneath · ABOUT 20 MINUTES

Why things move. And why they stop.

A tank crossing mud, a phone lighting up and the Moon staying in orbit all follow physical rules. Physics helps us describe those rules and make predictions we can test.

START WITH A QUESTION

A heavy tank has wide tracks. Why might it cross soft ground more easily than a much lighter vehicle with narrow wheels?

Have a guess together before revealing the idea.

The idea underneath +

Forces are interactions: pushes and pulls that can change motion or shape. Energy is a quantity we track as things change; it is transferred rather than used up. Models of forces, energy, matter and waves help explain events from a rolling ball to light arriving from a star.

Why know this?

Physics makes everyday technology less mysterious. It helps you think about stopping distances, insulation, electricity bills, lenses and whether a dramatic movie stunt makes sense.

01

Huge machine, surprisingly gentle footprint

Tracks spread weight over a larger contact area, reducing average ground pressure. Real mud and traction add more complications.

02

Recoil has a reason

When a gun pushes a projectile forwards, the projectile pushes the gun backwards. Forces come from interactions between objects.

03

Space is a silent cinema

Sound needs matter to travel through. Light can cross a vacuum, so a distant space explosion could be visible without its sound reaching you through empty space.

THINK / DRAW / TRY

Make it a conversation.

Press a rectangular eraser or block gently into modelling clay on its broad face, then its narrow face. Predict the deeper mark. Try to keep the pushing force the same. Draw the contact areas and discuss what made this comparison imperfect.

One more twist

If you doubled both the downward force and the contact area, what would happen to the average pressure?

Help me explain this +

Average pressure is force divided by area. Doubling both leaves it unchanged. Weight alone does not determine pressure. For the model, the challenge is applying the same force each time; noticing that limitation is good science.

A common mix-up

A moving object does not need a continuing forward force to keep moving at constant velocity. Everyday objects slow because interactions such as friction act on them.

Think like a scientist

Which variable did you change, which did you try to keep the same, and how could you make the comparison fairer?
